messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Vignette:
Martin Keller was 46 when he came for treatment, a married white American man who had worked for years as a graphic designer, most recently from a hybrid office where he split his time between home and a downtown studio. He described the trauma simply at first as “what happened with the police,” but when he tried to say more, his account repeatedly broke apart. He would begin with one image, jump to another, then stop altogether, visibly flooded, apologizing that he was losing the thread. What came across consistently was the scene itself: an encounter with police that had turned physical, close-range, and terrifying, leaving him with vivid images of injury that still felt present rather than past. What seemed to stay with him most sharply was the sight of wounds—blood, damaged skin, the unmistakable visual fact of someone hurt in front of him, and his helplessness in that moment with uniformed officers standing over the scene.

In the weeks afterward, Martin found that the event did not settle into memory. It returned as unwanted thoughts that pushed in when he was trying to work, talk with his wife, or do ordinary things around the house. At other times the memory seemed to come back all at once, without warning, as if something in the environment had opened a trapdoor beneath him. He could be walking through the city on his way to the studio, glance across the street, and see a police cruiser or an officer standing outside a storefront, and suddenly he was no longer just noticing a cop on the block; he was back inside that earlier moment, hit by the same surge of emotion so intensely that he had to stop what he was doing. The sight of visible injuries on other people could do the same thing. A scraped face on the subway, a bandaged hand in a coffee shop, even an image online that showed wounds too clearly could catch him off guard and bring the whole thing rushing back before he had any chance to brace himself.

Since then, Martin had come to live as though danger might break through at any time. Even in places he knew were safe, he said he could not relax. His body stayed keyed up, shoulders tight, jaw set, scanning the room before he could pay attention to anything else. At restaurants he automatically looked for the exits before sitting down. In his office building he noted stairwells, side doors, and where he might go if he had to get out fast. He did this so routinely that it now felt less like a choice than a condition for being anywhere at all. He knew, rationally, that his design meetings were not dangerous, but he did not feel safe in them until he had mapped the room.

Over months, Martin built his life around not having to sit still with his own mind. He stayed on his phone late into the night, scrolling, reading, watching clips he barely cared about, then shifting to games or random internet searches just to keep mental space occupied. During the workday, when a project paused or a file was exporting, he reached for another screen immediately. If there was quiet, he filled it. He had also started avoiding people. Some of this was practical on the surface—working from home more often, declining casual lunches, skipping social gatherings with friends—but his wife had noticed how much smaller his world had become. He told himself it was easier not to deal with anyone, easier not to risk being asked questions or being put in situations where he might see a police officer nearby or be confronted with some stray image of injury that would undo him in public.

What frightened Martin most in the present was not just the memory itself but what he had come to believe about his life since it happened. He said that nothing felt meaningful anymore. Work, which had once given him satisfaction, now felt mechanical, just another way to get through the day with his attention pinned to a screen. He was certain that the trauma had destroyed his life, not in a dramatic single sense but in the way it had hollowed out his days and changed how he moved through even ordinary places. He also returned again and again to the unfairness of it. What happened to him felt deeply unjust, and in his mind nothing meaningful had been done about it. That fact sat with him heavily, as if the event were still unresolved in the world as well as in him.

By the time he sought help, the strain was visible at home and at work. His wife had begun telling him that even when he was physically present, he seemed elsewhere—either shut off or braced for something. At the studio, he was still meeting deadlines, but he arranged his days to minimize contact and felt exposed whenever he had to go in person. He finally came after a recent incident in which he saw an officer near his office entrance and then, moments later, a man with a fresh facial injury on the sidewalk. The combination hit him so hard that he turned around, left the building, and spent hours on his phone in a nearby café trying to settle enough to go home. Sitting in treatment, Martin said he was afraid that this was all his life would be now: narrowed, tense, and meaningless. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to be able to remember what happened without feeling overwhelmed and to move through the world without always preparing to escape it.
